implementation_notes: Go has neither immutability nor field projection, so the realization is hand-written: a method with a value receiver mutates its own copy and returns it - `func (a Address) WithCity(city string) Address { a.City = city; return a }` - and a nested update calls the inner `With`, then wraps the result in the outer one. Slices, maps and pointer-owned data must be cloned at the boundary (`slices.Clone`) or the copy still shares its backing array; unexported fields are what make the discipline enforceable. A `Lens[S, A]` type (get/set closures plus composition) can be hand-written on Go 1.18+ generics and does exist in the ecosystem (IBM's fp-go ships `optics/lens`), but it cannot project fields generically, so every lens still needs hand-written getter and setter closures; use the plain `With` methods unless a path must really be passed around as data.
pitfalls: A value receiver copies the struct header, not the data behind slices, maps and pointers: without slices.Clone/maps.Clone the "new" value aliases the old one's storage.
Embedding a `sync.Mutex` or copying a struct that contains one violates Go's copylocks rule; the vet failure usually arrives long after the pattern was introduced.
Exported fields defeat the discipline entirely - any caller can mutate in place, so the With-methods are a convention rather than a guarantee.
